title: What a Genre Promises
objective: After this level you can explain why a genre works as a promise between filmmakers and audiences about what they will feel.
summary: A genre promises something familiar and something new. Long familiarity trains viewers' expectations, and studios liked genres because reused sets and steady teams made filmmaking quicker.

cards.headline: You know how a Western goes before the lights go down.
cards.body: Cowboys, a dusty town, a showdown. You haven't seen a single frame, and you already have a list. Most genres are named by their subject or setting: the Western, the gangster film, the police thriller, science fiction. The name on the poster is a kind of promise. What exactly does it promise?

cards.headline: Same again, but different
cards.body: Britannica puts the genre deal neatly: a genre promises a waiting audience something similar to what it has enjoyed before, and yet something quite new and different. That's the tightrope. All sameness and the film is a rerun. All newness and it breaks the promise you bought a ticket for. Think of your favorite pizza place trying one new topping, not turning into a sushi bar.

mascot.line: Keep this: a genre promises the familiar and the new at once. Every level in this chapter is that promise, one genre at a time.

cards.headline: You walk in already trained
cards.body: Viewers knew, to a great extent, what to expect from a genre film. They recognized its stars, or at least its characters, and years of watching had made them sensitive to its music, its lighting and its plot devices. A chord in the score or a shadow on a wall could tell them what was coming. Every film you watch in a genre quietly trains you for the next one.

cards.headline: Why studios loved a formula
cards.body: Genres also suited a factory. A studio that planned half a dozen police thrillers in one year could reuse sets, costumes and props, saving time and money. Better still, it could keep the same writers, directors, crews and actors on the same genre, so they built a routine. That routine often made filmmaking quicker and better from one film to the next. The promise to audiences doubled as a production plan.

cards.headline: The genre promise: understood
learned: A genre promises something familiar and something new
Familiarity trains viewers to read music, lighting and plot devices
Studios reused sets and kept steady teams on each genre

questions.prompt: According to Britannica, what does a film genre promise its audience?

options.label: Exactly the same story as the last hit
options.rationale: Pure sameness would be a rerun; the promise includes something new.

options.label: Something familiar, yet also something new
A story never told in any form before
options.rationale: Pure newness would break the promise of the familiar.

options.label: Famous stars in every single role
options.rationale: Stars help, but the promise is about the kind of experience.

questions.explanation: Genres promise something similar to what audiences enjoyed before, and yet something quite new and different.

questions.prompt: Why could a studio that made six police thrillers in one year work faster and often better?

options.label: The law gave genre films shorter shooting schedules
options.rationale: No law was involved; the savings came from routine.

options.label: Critics reviewed genre films more kindly
options.rationale: The level is about production, not reviews.

options.label: It reused sets and kept the same teams, who built a routine
Audiences paid higher prices for genre films
options.rationale: The level says nothing about ticket prices.

questions.explanation: Reusing sets, costumes and props saved money, and keeping the same writers, directors, crews and actors on a genre built a routine.

questions.prompt: Level 8's The Great Train Robbery helped make the Western a staple. How did a steady stream of Westerns shape the audiences who watched them?

options.label: It made them tired of cowboys, so studios stopped
options.rationale: The Western became a staple, not a flop.

options.label: It taught them to ignore a film's music and lighting
options.rationale: Familiarity made viewers more sensitive to those, not less.

options.label: It made every new Western a complete surprise
Long familiarity taught them what to expect from each new one

questions.explanation: Viewers who had seen many films of a genre knew what to expect and were sensitive to its characters, music, lighting and plot devices.
